passages.text: Mechanical Impedance and Its Relations to Motor Control, Limb Dynamics, and Motion Biomechanics

The concept of mechanical impedance represents the interactive relationship between deformation kinematics and the resulting dynamics in human joints or limbs. <sentence_start/>A major component of impedance, stiffness, is defined as the ratio between the force change to the displacement change and is strongly related to muscle activation. <sentence_start/>The set of impedance components, including effective mass, inertia, damping, and stiffness, is important in determining the performance of the many tasks assigned to the limbs and in counteracting undesired effects of applied loads and disturbances. <sentence_start/>Specifically for the upper limb, impedance enables controlling manual tasks and reaching motions. <sentence_start/>In the lower limb, impedance is responsible for the transmission and attenuation of impact forces in tasks of repulsive loadings. <sentence_start/>This review presents an updated account of the works on mechanical impedance and its relations with motor control, limb dynamics, and motion biomechanics. <sentence_start/>Basic questions related to the linearity and nonlinearity of impedance and to the factors that affect mechanical impedance are treated with relevance to upper and lower limb functions, joint performance, trunk stability, and seating under dynamic conditions. <sentence_start/>Methods for the derivation of mechanical impedance, both those for within the system and material-structural approaches, are reviewed. <sentence_start/>For system approaches, special attention is given to methods aimed at revealing the correct and sufficient degree of nonlinearity of impedance. <sentence_start/>This is particularly relevant in the design of spring-based artificial legs and robotic arms. <sentence_start/>Finally, due to the intricate relation between impedance and muscle activity, methods for the explicit expression of impedance of contractile tissue are reviewed.
Introduction: Redundancy, Mechanical Indeterminacy, and Lumping

The human motor system benefits from remarkable neuro-muscular redundancies. <sentence_start/>A motor task is normally performed with the concurrent involvement of more muscles than seemingly required. <sentence_start/>Further, a given task may be performed in multiple ways, each involving different motor units from several muscles that have to be orderly activated and coordinated. <sentence_start/>It has been demonstrated that the central nervous system makes use of simplifying strategies to facilitate complex tasks through the creation of muscle synergies that are put together by the motor cortical area and afferent systems [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR1" doi="10.3389/fncom.2013.00051" pmcid="PMC3638124" pmid="23641212" count="1">1</citation>]. <sentence_start/>From the mechanical viewpoint, the musculoskeletal system is indeterminate, with the number of unknown muscle forces exceeding the number of available equations [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2" count="1">2</citation>].

The origin of neuro-muscular redundancy is expressed in the descending pathways from the central nervous system to the peripheral one. <sentence_start/>As a matter of fact, there exist multiple pathways for the execution of a given motor task such that the same information may be processed in different ways. <sentence_start/>Thus, a given central command may result in different activation combinations and, conversely, different commands can result in the same activation scheme. <sentence_start/>A trivial example arises when a joint torque of required intensity is to be provided. <sentence_start/>This torque can be produced in an infinite number of ways, involving co-contraction of the antagonist muscles at various activation intensities. <sentence_start/>From the purely mechanical aspect, the existence of co-contraction is actually undesirable because it results in a larger net joint force. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, co-contraction is physiologically beneficial because it facilitates stability and controllability of posture and motion, sometimes at the cost of accelerated fatigue [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" pmid="9460158" doi="10.1097/00007632-199801010-00019" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An interesting issue relates to the possibility to unequivocally resolve the muscle forces from the estimated joint torques. <sentence_start/>The redundancy of the musculoskeletal system provides numerous possible solutions to the problem of partitioning torque among active muscles [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4" count="1">4</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR5" count="1">5</citation>].

Thus, indeterminacy is associated with a multitude of possible solutions of the available system of equations. <sentence_start/>Conventional methods of addressing mechanical indeterminacy usually refer to the implementation of optimization criteria [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR6" pmid="7276011" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(81)90001-4" count="1">6</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7" pmid="7704345" doi="10.1016/1350-4533(95)90378-o" count="1">7</citation>], providing supplementary equations that allow eliminating irrelevant solutions. <sentence_start/>Nonetheless, the level of indeterminacy is expected to decrease with the reduction of redundancy [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8" pmid="17350288" doi="10.1016/j.jelekin.2007.01.009" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this respect, information about the activities of the muscles as expressed by their electromyograms (EMGs) may be instrumental in resolving muscle and joint forces and other unknowns from the musculoskeletal mechanical equations [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR2" count="1">2</citation>].

Indeterminacy of the locomotor system can also be addressed by implementing the lumping method, whereby the material elements of the human body, e.g., muscles, tendons, ligaments, bones, and joints, are lumped together in functional units so that the overall musculoskeletal system is represented as a one or more degrees-of-freedom (DOFs) damped elastic mechanism, interconnecting the masses of the body segments [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This method has been implemented for the modeling of various physical activities, including reaching motion for the upper limb [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" pmid="4045550" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.05-10-02732.1985" pmcid="PMC6565149" count="1">10</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>] or, for the lower limbs, walking, hopping, and running. <sentence_start/>In this latter case, the foot- or heel-strike period during the landing phase has been modeled by means of one-dimensional lumped models (with linear displacements) or rotational lumping (with angular displacements) [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1115/1.3138305" pmid="7078120" count="1">15</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR23" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(98)00145-6" pmid="10327006" count="1">23</citation>].

The idea of lumping has also been applied to the multi-segmental modeling of bilateral standing sway and standing imbalance [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR24" count="1">24</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR29" count="1">29</citation>] and the modeling of standing on one leg [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4" count="1">4</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR8" pmid="17350288" doi="10.1016/j.jelekin.2007.01.009" count="1">8</citation>].

The rest of this review is organized as follows. <sentence_start/>Section 2 presents the concept of mechanical impedance and the conditions where it may be treated as a constant or a variable property, thus giving rise to nonlinearities such as those in repulsive tasks or in human joints. <sentence_start/>Section 3 deals with the derivation of equations from which the mechanical impedance can be resolved and with methods of solutions of these equations. <sentence_start/>Section 4 lists the factors affecting mechanical impedance, including muscle activation, pre-programming of muscle activity, weight bearing, body configuration, types of interface between body and environment, nature of performed tasks, learning, and fatigue. <sentence_start/>Section 5 presents the intrinsic expression of mechanical impedance derived from the tissue level, as opposed to the system level, and expands this notion for the explicit expression of the impedance for contractile tissue. <sentence_start/>Finally, section 6 concludes the review by highlighting the relevance of mechanical impedance to control strategies of movement and the design of artificial legs and robots.
Concept of Mechanical Impedance
Definition

The complex relationship between deformation kinematics (generalized displacement/velocity) and the resulting dynamics (generalized force/torque), is termed mechanical impedance and defines the linear or rotational stiffness and damping characteristics of the system under consideration. <sentence_start/>The concept of impedance was first introduced in mechanical problems by Firestone [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR30" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In its simplest form, stiffness is defined as the ratio between the force change to the displacement change [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR31" pmid="21396646" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2011.02.072" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The impedance components (stiffness, effective mass, and damping) are particularly important for limb function since they counteract the effects of applied loads and disturbances.

In fact, a distinction should be made between impedance and admittance: while the first relates input kinematics to the resulting output dynamics of the system, the second relates the input dynamics to the resulting output kinematics. <sentence_start/>The electrical analogy of these two terms is with resistance and conductance which, like in mechanical systems, are also frequency-dependent. <sentence_start/>In linear systems, these two representations are usually equivalent and interchangeable. <sentence_start/>However, in nonlinear problems, such as those related to object manipulation, these two are not interchangeable [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32" count="1">32</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For instance, for a hybrid controller implemented in the design of a torque-controlled manipulator to identify the dynamics of the wrist joint, the inertia and damping were implemented via admittance, and the stiffness via impedance [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33" pmid="16434105" doi="10.1016/j.jneumeth.2005.12.001" count="1">33</citation>].
Average Impedance

A simpler definition of impedance makes reference to average stiffness, defined as the ratio between generalized force (force or torque) to overall generalized displacement (linear or angular) for the system under consideration (limb or joint). <sentence_start/>Similarly, average damping is obtained as the ratio between generalized force and generalized displacement rate.

In a review of spring-damper lumped systems, models were categorized as being either passive or active [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34" doi="10.1177/0954411911424210" pmid="22320052" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In passive models, the mechanical properties (stiffness and damping) were treated as being constant, and in active models, the mechanical properties were considered to adapt to external loads [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR34" doi="10.1177/0954411911424210" pmid="22320052" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This categorization contradicts, however, other studies, which showed that nonlinearities of stiffness and damping can be found also in the passive state.
Past studies have modeled the human body using lumped components with constant average stiffnesses. <sentence_start/>Some examples are given below.
Vibrating Seats and Vehicles

This category includes multiple-DOF linear models of a seated vehicle driver [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR35" doi="10.1115/1.3138671" pmid="3657108" count="1">35</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR37" pmid="7464277" doi="10.1007/BF02443126" count="1">37</citation>], shipboard sitting subject to underwater shock [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR38" pmid="11747881" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(01)00167-1" count="1">38</citation>], seated pregnant women for examination of the vibration effect on the woman and fetus under both horizontal and vertical vibrations [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR39" pmid="8818132" doi="10.1016/1350-4533(95)00060-7" count="1">39</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR40" pmid="8964779" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(95)00074-7" count="1">40</citation>], and seated wheelchair users [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR41" pmid="12018649" doi="10.1109/TNSRE.2001.1000116" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Using the electrical analogy method for solution, it was found that horizontal vibrations affect body segments more than do vertical vibrations [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR40" pmid="8964779" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(95)00074-7" count="1">40</citation>].

With specific reference to seating design, an attempt was made to develop human body protection devices, such as cushions or seats with a shock absorber, in a vibration environment with a multiple-DOF lumped parameter model representing a seated human body/seat system and comprising the following two components: a global one, which included a systematic set of the model parameters for simulating various conditions such as body posture, backrest, footrest, muscle tension, and vibration directions; and a local one, which represented the human pelvis/vibrating seat contact, using a cushioning interface [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR42" doi="10.1115/1.1559894" pmid="12751284" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The very common seated position, particularly in the presence of vibrations, such as during the driving of a vehicle, is a subject of continuing interest as it is often related to the development of discomfort and back pain and spine disorders. <sentence_start/>Questions related to small-moderate variability of backrest inclination and backrest foam insertion, of position of the limbs while seated, and of the vibration conditions were shown to be satisfactorily addressed by a single-DOF lumped parameter model describing the vertical apparent mass of the human body. <sentence_start/>For example, contact with a rigid backrest, which is expected to reduce the vibrating mass and increase stiffness, resulted in an increase in the derived damped natural frequency of the principal resonance. <sentence_start/>An increase in the backrest inclination, which is also expected to reduce the moving mass, caused a decrease in the damping and an increase in the resonance frequency [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR43" pmid="20953082" doi="10.2486/indhealth.mswbvi-33" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In search for criteria for developing active and passive isolation mechanisms for reducing the effects of whole-body vibration exposure while seated, one study developed a three-mass, two-DOF model that revealed nonlinear stiffness properties whereby the mean stiffness coefficients and the mean undamped natural frequencies associated with the upper torso and leg subsystems showed a significant decrease with increasing acceleration level [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR44" pmid="8060029" doi="10.1007/BF02368224" count="1">44</citation>].
Upper Limb

In the design of a torque-controlled manipulator, the wrist dynamics was described by a second-order inertia-spring-damper system and no distinction was made between muscle viscoelasticity and reflexive stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR33" pmid="16434105" doi="10.1016/j.jneumeth.2005.12.001" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An apparatus was developed to quantify the average dynamic mechanical properties during active muscle exertions by delivering an external perturbation to the upper limb through a handle. <sentence_start/>The mechanical stiffness, damping, and effective mass elements were determined from free vibration displacement by calculating the frequency changes of the externally loaded system [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR45" pmid="16076739" doi="10.1080/00140130500142209" count="1">45</citation>].

For the hand-arm system, early modeling with constant impedance made use of a two-DOF representation of the elbow-wrist joints with linear impedances to describe the dynamic response to vibration input to the hand and revealed that the hand-arm system may be viewed as a low-pass mechanical filter that attenuates high frequencies [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR12" pmid="11699114" doi="10.1037/0033-295x.108.4.709" count="1">12</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR13" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A dynamic model of the biomechanics of the index finger including all the tendons and their varying moment arms assumed a constant stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR7" pmid="7704345" doi="10.1016/1350-4533(95)90378-o" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finger impedance measurements made under perturbations fast enough to prevent spinal reflex interference during data acquisition also assumed constant impedance [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR46" pmid="21863387" doi="10.1007/s10439-011-0381-7" count="1">46</citation>].
Models for Physical Activities of Repulsive Tasks

These models have provided, to a limited extent, reasonable prediction of the foot-ground reaction forces while using lumped models with constant-average-stiffness elastic springs and negligible or no viscous damping [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1115/1.3138305" pmid="7078120" count="1">15</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21" pmid="8849811" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(95)00029-1" count="1">21</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22" pmid="10093026" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(98)00170-5" count="1">22</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47" pmid="10569714" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00133-5" count="1">47</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR50" pmid="2081746" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(90)90042-2" count="1">50</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For running jumps for height and distance, segmental wobbling mass modeling was used to determine the elastic parameters of segments and the foot-ground interface [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR51" pmid="16002080" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.05.012" count="1">51</citation>].
Models for Carrying Backpacks

Lumped models simulating the interaction between the human trunk and a carried backpack using constant impedance values have been developed [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR52" pmid="19062021" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2008.10.012" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Backpack dynamics has been described using a nonlinear suspension model within whole body motion analysis during carrying. <sentence_start/>It was found that decreasing suspension stiffness moderated the peak values of vertical backpack force, acting on the trunk and lower limb joints. <sentence_start/>This reduced shoulder strap pressures and the risk of injury when heavy loads were carried. <sentence_start/>It was also found that the backpack suspension stiffness and damping have little effect on human locomotion energetics [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR53" pmid="15713307" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.04.030" count="1">53</citation>].
Spine Models

Numerous lumped models of the spine structure with constant impedance values have been developed. <sentence_start/>For example, a five-DOF lumped equivalent model with constant impedance values was developed for the lumbar spine [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR54" pmid="12381970" doi="10.1067/mmt.2002.127079" count="1">54</citation>], from which the postero-anterior motion could be predicted in the static, cyclic, and impulsive force modes.
Variable Impedance

Linear models fail to predict the true dynamic response of the modeled systems. <sentence_start/>The use of invariable mechanical stiffness may not be physiologically applicable, as stiffness nonlinearity is important in stabilizing elastic chains during dynamic loading [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55" pmid="11357549" doi="10.1007/PL00007982" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Joint impedance has thus been treated as a nonlinear phenomenon [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR56" doi="10.1007/BF00430956" pmid="598364" count="1">56</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR58" pmid="8253830" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(93)90073-n" count="1">58</citation>].

It has been claimed that the determination of constant-value stiffness and damping coefficients is an ill-posed problem and that small errors in the measured kinematic data (i.e., noise, time delays) will lead to large errors in the estimated variables [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR59" pmid="2049415" doi="10.1007/BF00224708" count="1">59</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR60" pmid="21637750" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0019568" pmcid="PMC3103502" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It has thus been suggested that parameter estimation should rather be conducted using a moving-time-window algorithm, resulting in impedance values that are influenced not only by the nature of the perturbation but also by the time window over which the parameters are estimated [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR60" pmid="21637750" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0019568" pmcid="PMC3103502" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A time-window method was implemented to determine the time-dependent changes in joint stiffness, damping, and equilibrium position in human forearm movements based on data of a single movement [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61" pmid="10529503" doi="10.1123/mcj.3.4.394" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be noted, however, that although stiffness and damping in a stiffness-damping-inertia model is a nonlinear mixture of all the dynamic parameters of the musculoskeletal model, for practical purposes model representation of the impedance redundancies can be reduced to less cumbersome nonlinearities [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>].
Physical Activities of Repulsive Tasks
Hopping

Repulsive tasks such as human hopping, jumping, and running were studied by assuming position-dependent and/or angle-dependent joint stiffnesses in three-segment models [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR55" pmid="11357549" doi="10.1007/PL00007982" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Damping, though generally not negligible, was found to be low. <sentence_start/>More specifically, for hopping motion, rotational springs with nonlinear stiffnesses in a four-segment leg model revealed that the correct and sufficient variability of the joint stiffness is of first order (i.e., linearly variable with joint angle) [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>].

Muscular activation level, which in hopping motion determines the ability of the muscle-tendon complex to absorb, store, release, and generate energy, varies during the stance phase. <sentence_start/>Since the stiffness generally depends on the activation level of the muscle [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR3" pmid="9460158" doi="10.1097/00007632-199801010-00019" count="1">3</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62" pmid="17196827" doi="10.1016/j.jelekin.2006.10.010" count="1">62</citation>], it follows that hopping cannot be treated as a purely harmonic motion and that human joints are not simple mechanical springs.
Running

For the stance phase of human running, the leg was modeled as a one-dimensional four-DOF lumped system [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Departing from the constant-stiffness concept, the model revealed that a correct and sufficient variability of the joint stiffness is a two-region piece-wise constant joint stiffness, indicating that a higher order of nonlinearity is unnecessary. <sentence_start/>This result should be considered meaningful for problems where the constant stiffness representation is insufficient and in cases where the system’s representation has to be improved. <sentence_start/>As already mentioned, joint stiffness is dominated by muscular activation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR63" count="1">63</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR64" pmid="3410857" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90217-5" count="1">64</citation>] and as the joints stiffen, they experience a decrease in angular displacements during the ground-contact phase, resulting in smaller excursion of the hip and higher leg stiffness. <sentence_start/>Solutions obtained using piece-wise constant stiffness provide, through the obtained stiffness profiles, an insight into the patterns of the muscular activation in the legs’ joints. <sentence_start/>A simple model with a piece-wise constant stiffness can predict major features of running, making it an effective tool for the design of artificial legs and robots and also for the development of more accurate control strategies.
It was also reported that during heel strike, the joints did not have a damping effect, and thus did not contribute to energy dissipation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" count="1">9</citation>].
Ankle Joint

The complexity of the ankle joint presents an interesting challenge for modeling and resolving mechanical impedance. <sentence_start/>Considering first the mechanics of this joint in the sagittal plane, i.e., with the motion taking place in plantar and dorsi flexion of the joint, the relationship between the applied external moment and the resulting angular displacement can be studied in oscillatory motion, in which the foot is driven relative to the shank with the torque being applied by means of a band-limited oscillatory Gaussian signal [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65" pmid="690152" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(78)90010-6" count="1">65</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This setting also allows studying the effects on mechanical impedance of the activation level of the muscles around the joint, and of the dynamic reflex as a result of applying a sudden torque. <sentence_start/>Variations in the resting posture of the tested subject, the mode of attachment of the foot, and the manner of applying the displacement perturbations to the foot were later introduced to this method [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66" pmid="7153228" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90090-2" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The amplitude of motion and fatigue of the muscles during exercise were found to be of considerable significance to mechanical impedance values.

Further, by applying stochastic perturbation of the ankle angular position for actively exerting plantar or dorsi flexion torques, mechanical impedance was evaluated in the ankle joint for a range of muscle activation levels. <sentence_start/>It was found that while the elastic stiffness proportionally increased with the mean torque at all levels of muscle activation, damping remained almost invariant over the entire range of contractions [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR64" pmid="3410857" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90217-5" count="1">64</citation>].

The above studies about the ankle joint in plantar/dorsi flexion motion made use of a second-order quasi-linear underdamped system, by which elastic stiffness, damping coefficient, natural frequency, and moment of inertia of the foot about the ankle joint could be evaluated. <sentence_start/>Stiffness and damping characteristics of the ankle joint plantar flexors were not affected by static stretching [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR67" count="1">67</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR68" count="1">68</citation>].

For the subtalar joint, statically evaluating the stiffness of various football boots in inversion-eversion motion revealed that when using rigidly attached high boots, ligamentous load on the subtalar joint was reduced considerably, indicating conditions under which footwear may protect the joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR60" pmid="21637750" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0019568" pmcid="PMC3103502" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For that same joint, for an unexpected and sudden inversion motion of the foot, it was reported that the stretch reflex on the peroneal muscles remains unelicited for a period of approximately 70 ms from the onset of motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, the dynamic properties of the human subtalar joint in sudden inversion motion, which is likely to occur in conditions of inversion sprain of the ankle joint, were studied in vivo on a specially designed apparatus [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This joint was modeled as a quasi-linear second-order underdamped system, from which the elastic stiffness and damping coefficient, the natural frequency of the foot, and its moment of inertia about the joint were evaluated. <sentence_start/>The variation of mechanical impedance with joint angle was confirmed [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>].

Stiffness, damping, and inertia parameters were also studied in three- and four-DOF models of the lower limb in torsion, in which a dynamic pulse loading was applied at the foot-boot level [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" pmid="3417692" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90146-7" count="1">71</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR72" pmid="7096375" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90254-8" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For rotation motion, the dynamics of the ankle in the medial-lateral plane in both laboratory and skiing apparatuses was studied to identify stiffness, damping, and inertia parameters [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR72" pmid="7096375" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90254-8" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Weight bearing on the foot and muscle-induced torsion were used as test variables, and were found to be important in studying the dynamics of the ankle. <sentence_start/>Comparing this model with a more simplified single-DOF model, which best duplicates the rotation of the knee, indicated that the latter model gave good prediction of knee rotation, with stiffness symmetrical with respect to the rotation direction [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" pmid="3417692" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90146-7" count="1">71</citation>].
Upper Limb

The mechanical impedance of the upper limb is of great interest because of the many tasks assigned to the upper limb, including manual tasks (such as grasping and/or using hand and power tools) and reaching motions. <sentence_start/>Prior to a detailed discussion on these tasks, it should be mentioned that torsional pendulum tests were implemented on the upper limb, allowing limb inertia and muscle stiffness to be calculated [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR73" pmid="3588828" doi="10.1113/expphysiol.1987.sp003060" count="1">73</citation>].
Grasping Objects and Reaching Motion

Numerous studies have modeled grasping and reaching motion. <sentence_start/>With the objective to map the field of restoring forces associated with posture in the horizontal plane of the multiarticular arm, small displacements along various directions were delivered to the hand [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" pmid="4045550" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.05-10-02732.1985" pmcid="PMC6565149" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Measured force and displacement vectors before the onset of voluntary reaction were used to estimate the stiffness in the vicinity of the hand equilibrium position. <sentence_start/>It was found that the forces were predominantly conservative, indicating a spring-like behavior of the neuromuscular system. <sentence_start/>A defined stiffness ellipse, representing the main geometrical features of the elastic force field, was defined as follows: the major and minor axes were scaled to the maximum and minimum stiffness, respectively; the ellipse area was scaled to the total stiffness, and the orientation of the ellipse was made to coincide with the direction of the major (or minor) axis. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, the obtained ellipse field was found to be invariant among the tested subjects and over time of testing. <sentence_start/>Further, when a disturbance acting along a fixed and predictable direction was imposed, the magnitude of the total stiffness increased but only minor changes in shape and orientation occurred, shedding light on neural factors involved in maintaining hand posture [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" pmid="4045550" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.05-10-02732.1985" pmcid="PMC6565149" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Measuring the postural force field of a subject’s arm over relatively large distances, and comparing these forces with the static forces generated at the hand while the subject attempted a reaching movement, confirmed the hypothesis that the central nervous system programs a reaching movement by shifting the equilibrium position of the hand toward the target [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR74" pmid="8423483" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.13-01-00045.1993" pmcid="PMC6576309" count="1">74</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, due to the large displacements from equilibrium, the use of a nonlinear model (i.e., a variable stiffness matrix) is required to describe the measured postural field [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR74" pmid="8423483" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.13-01-00045.1993" pmcid="PMC6576309" count="1">74</citation>].

As later shown, during simple point-to-point movement, the human arm did not behave in a conservative manner and could not even be described as a stable passive dynamic system around a desired trajectory. <sentence_start/>In fact, muscle properties and automatic reflex response can result in significant deviations from the desired trajectory, with over-compensation in the form of an active response [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR75" count="1">75</citation>].
Grasping Objects and Locomotion

An interesting problem presents when grasping takes place simultaneously with locomotion, requiring the coordination of these two modes of control [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR76" count="1">76</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR78" pmid="16874513" doi="10.1007/s00221-006-0618-0" count="1">78</citation>]. <sentence_start/>More specifically, the effect of constraint of the joints of the upper limb was studied to shed light on the mechanisms of stabilization of manually held objects during walking through impedance adjustments [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This was performed by successively immobilizing each of the joints while subjects walked steadily with a hand-held cup filled with liquid. <sentence_start/>The ability to maintain the liquid level was used to indicate how well the limb navigated itself to minimize liquid spillage from the cup and how the limb adapted to the imposed joint restrictions. <sentence_start/>This problem has strong relevance in impedance-based control strategies and provides an insight into the mechanisms by which stiffness and damping are adjusted to accommodate changes taking place during manual transport of objects while aiming to ensure their stability during walking.

A two-dimensional sagittal model consisting of three segments, namely upper arm, forearm, and hand connected together by the joints via lumped parameter impedances representing damped springs, was thus set to describe the system. <sentence_start/>The semi-repetitive oscillations of the shoulder girdle produced by the ambulatory mechanism in concert with the motion of the joints of the upper limb navigated the hand holding the cup of liquid in an oscillatory-like motion. <sentence_start/>With the gait-generated motion of the shoulder girdle and limb serving as inputs to the model and the kinematics of the hand holding the fluid filled cup serving as output, the impedance adjustments were resolved during the simultaneous control of grasping and walking under ordinary conditions, and when each one of the joints is immobilized.
Neck Modeling in Impact Motion

A lumped model to describe neck behavior in low-velocity rear-end impact implemented on a dummy satisfactorily predicted the response when elastic stiffness and damping were combined in the muscle substitutes with a nonlinear stiffness of model joints [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR79" pmid="10688482" doi="10.1016/s0001-4575(99)00085-8" count="1">79</citation>].
Derivation of Equations for Dynamic Model
Nature of Driving Perturbation

Impedance values can be generally derived from the dynamic equations of motion, through which relationships between the driving perturbation and the resulting response can be obtained. <sentence_start/>Methods can be grouped according to the mode of applied driving force or displacement perturbation as follows.
Oscillatory Methods

A common method to resolve mechanical impedance from oscillatory motion was implemented in the wrist joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR80" pmid="16125181" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.06.022" count="1">80</citation>] and ankle joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65" pmid="690152" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(78)90010-6" count="1">65</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this latter case, the foot was driven relative to the shank and the torque was delivered by means of a band-limited oscillatory Gaussian signal. <sentence_start/>This provided the relationship between the applied external moment and the resulting angular displacement of the joint. <sentence_start/>Oscillatory methods were also used to study the biomechanical characteristics of the muscles of the human ankle joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR81" pmid="6540667" doi="10.1007/BF00943370" count="1">81</citation>] and the human arm [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR82" pmid="13997862" count="1">82</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR83" doi="10.1109/IEMBS.2010.5627544" pmid="21096937" count="1">83</citation>].
Impact Perturbation

A fast forward head movement in the frontal plane was modeled to study head-neck joint response [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR84" pmid="15316785" doi="10.1007/s00422-004-0481-7" count="1">84</citation>]. <sentence_start/>If the perturbation is fast enough, the effect of the accompanied muscular activity can be neutralized. <sentence_start/>A method to accomplish that was devised for inversion motion of the subtalar joint by suddenly and unexpectedly rotating the foot relative to the shank on a specially constructed swiveling platform, driven by stretched springs. <sentence_start/>If motion lasts less than 40 ms, the protective muscles are not elicited by the stretch reflex [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR69" count="1">69</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The impedance properties obtained from this experiment represent the passive properties of the ankle joint in inversion/eversion motion in sprain-like conditions of the ankle. <sentence_start/>Using appropriate instrumentation, information about torque and kinematics can be obtained [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The same idea of preventing the stretch reflex by sufficiently fast perturbations was applied for measuring human finger impedance [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR46" pmid="21863387" doi="10.1007/s10439-011-0381-7" count="1">46</citation>].

muscle stiffness to be calculated [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR73" pmid="3588828" doi="10.1113/expphysiol.1987.sp003060" count="1">73</citation>].
Static, Dynamic, and Creep Tests

Static, dynamic, and creep tests of the human knee in vivo were performed to estimate the viscoelastic properties of the knee [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR94" pmid="939766" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(76)90087-7" count="1">94</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The dynamic disturbance was provided by means of a sinusoidal displacement generator to excite the knee-leg system and the driving force was monitored as a function of the frequency and mechanical characteristics of the knee. <sentence_start/>It was found that in quasi-static loading, the knee exhibited hysteresis. <sentence_start/>In dynamic loading, the knee behaved as a single-DOF spring-mass-damper system with a St. Venant’s friction element [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR94" pmid="939766" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(76)90087-7" count="1">94</citation>].
