Governing Equations

The dynamics of interconnected lumped segments can be expressed using Newton-Euler equations of motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1115/1.3138305" pmid="7078120" count="1">15</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR26" pmid="9652081" doi="10.1007/s004220050436" count="1">26</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR59" pmid="2049415" doi="10.1007/BF00224708" count="1">59</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>] and inverse-dynamics methods, such as for impact loading of the lower leg [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" count="1">9</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>] or step loading of the elbow [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR98" pmid="21484509" doi="10.1007/s10439-011-0308-3" count="1">98</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Alternatively, velocity-based inverse-dynamics equations using Kane’s [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR99" count="1">99</citation>] method can be used. <sentence_start/>For single-stance standing, open-chain inverse-dynamics was used [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR4" count="1">4</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR100" count="1">100</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR101" count="1">101</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The governing equations for expressing the mechanical impedances in lumped systems can be categorized as follows.
Second-Order System

Second-order quasi-linear underdamped systems have been used for oscillatory motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65" pmid="690152" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(78)90010-6" count="1">65</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66" pmid="7153228" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90090-2" count="1">66</citation>], impact motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR15" doi="10.1115/1.3138305" pmid="7078120" count="1">15</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>], and isotonic loading of the trunk [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR62" pmid="17196827" doi="10.1016/j.jelekin.2006.10.010" count="1">62</citation>] to evaluate elastic stiffness, damping coefficient, natural frequency, and moment of inertia. <sentence_start/>Such systems were implemented for the ankle joint in plantar and dorsi flexion motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR65" pmid="690152" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(78)90010-6" count="1">65</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66" pmid="7153228" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90090-2" count="1">66</citation>], the wrist joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR80" pmid="16125181" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.06.022" count="1">80</citation>], and the trunk using the load sudden-release method [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR102" pmid="19062020" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2008.10.001" count="1">102</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Active extension exertions were also used in the trunk to estimate the active impedance component values using second-order trunk dynamics following preload that caused small amplitude trunk movements [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR103" pmid="16084200" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.09.014" pmcid="PMC1630678" count="1">103</citation>].
Regressive Function

Regressive functions can be used to express stiffness and damping in terms of joint angle and joint angular velocity. <sentence_start/>For instance, it has been found that for the upper limb joints during grasping control taking place simultaneously with walking motion, stiffness includes first-order dependence on angle and angular velocity. <sentence_start/>The function used for damping included first-order dependence on angular velocity [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For the lower limb, it was found that during hopping motion, stiffness included second-order dependence on angle and first-order dependence on angular velocity and that damping was negligible [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The logic behind representing such a regressive function stems from the fact that the mechanical properties of a biological material can, in general, be multiple-variable-dependent. <sentence_start/>Specifically, stiffness, in addition to being nonlinear (e.g., strain-dependent), may often depend on the deformation rate. <sentence_start/>This is the case with bones [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR104" doi="10.1007/BF02477046" pmid="994579" count="1">104</citation>], tendons and ligaments [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR105" doi="10.1002/jor.1100080513" pmid="2388111" count="1">105</citation>], cartilage [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR106" count="1">106</citation>], and muscle [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR107" pmid="1791180" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(91)90375-w" count="1">107</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similarly, damping can be position-dependent. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, stiffness and damping during the stance phase of hopping can be represented by a general second-order regressive function.
Additional Methods

Alternative methods include using an artificial neural network for the prediction of the biodynamic response during vertical vibration of the seated human body in a sitting posture without a backrest [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR97" count="1">97</citation>].
Methods of Solution

The stiffness and damping coefficients can be resolved from the governing equations by parameter estimation using optimization procedures such as minimization of an objective function for each of the joints.

The model parameters should be independent of each other and, if multiple linear regression analyses are performed, for the parameter estimation to be correct all predictor variables must be uncorrelated. <sentence_start/>In the numerical solution procedure, it is thus necessary to reveal dependencies and eliminate redundancies of the stiffness and damping coefficients. <sentence_start/>This may be done using multicollinearity diagnostic algorithms combined with <italic toggle="yes">F</italic>-test [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR108" doi="10.1152/ajpregu.1985.249.1.R1" pmid="4014489" count="1">108</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Parameter identification can be performed using either quadratic programming [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR109" count="1">109</citation>] or a genetic algorithm [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR110" count="1">110</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Two examples are given below.
Hopping Motion

In hopping motion, after eliminating redundancies in the numerical solution using the above-mentioned multicollinearity diagnostic algorithms, the model revealed that the correct and sufficient variability of the joint stiffness is of first order, indicating that a higher order of nonlinearity is not necessary [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This result should be considered meaningful in problems where a constant stiffness representation is insufficient and in cases where the system’s representation has to be improved. <sentence_start/>The variable stiffness solution also provides, through the obtained stiffness profiles, an insight into the patterns of the muscular activation in the legs’ joints.

The fact that the simple model of a linearly variable stiffness can predict major features of the jumping exercise makes it an effective tool for future design of artificial legs and robots and also for the development of more accurate control strategies.
Simultaneous Grasping and Locomotion

The results obtained in the cup of liquid problem, in which the spring coefficients were expressed in terms of the joint angles and angular velocities, indicated a continuous nonlinear behavior of the joints. <sentence_start/>This sheds light on the design of spring-based artificial and robotic arms [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The wrist joint was found to have constant stiffness and damping and thus no regulation of these coefficients was necessary during gait. <sentence_start/>This is consistent with results for moderately sized wrist rotations, indicating that a simple, linear model can be used for studies in biomechanics, motor neuroscience, and rehabilitation, neglecting nonlinearities [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR111" pmid="21130996" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2010.11.016" count="1">111</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The passive stiffness of the wrist is sufficient to account for the pattern of the path of rotation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR112" pmid="22131378" doi="10.1152/jn.00428.2011" count="1">112</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Dominance of the passive viscoelastic (particularly the stiffness component) torques in planar wrist movements was also confirmed [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR113" pmid="22156946" doi="10.1109/TBME.2011.2178240" count="1">113</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings somewhat contradict earlier ones, indicating that while the muscle properties around the wrist were basically spring-like, there are major nonlinearities in the viscoelastic properties of the wrist [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR114" pmid="6534226" doi="10.1007/BF02371452" count="1">114</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Testing the wrist using the vibration method revealed that the stiffness, viscosity, and damping ratio decreased significantly across all displacements, with higher values for small angles and lower values with increasing flexion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR80" pmid="16125181" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.06.022" count="1">80</citation>].

Both in the elbow and shoulder joints, stiffness included a constant coefficient as well as an angular-velocity-dependent coefficient, with no damping. <sentence_start/>These results confirmed that, in this case, a higher order of nonlinearity was not necessary.
Factors that Affect Mechanical Impedance

The ability to tune and/or control the mechanical impedance of the limb joints is an important feature of the neuromuscular system [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR32" count="1">32</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR115" count="1">115</citation>] and of multi-joint powered orthotics [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR116" pmid="9535529" doi="10.1109/86.662626" count="1">116</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Tuning of the mechanical impedance facilitates, for example, the stabilization of hand-held objects in space, or the attenuation of undesired shock loads resulting from externally applied forces [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11" pmid="10592022" doi="10.1007/s004220050577" count="1">11</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR46" pmid="21863387" doi="10.1007/s10439-011-0381-7" count="1">46</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR117" count="1">117</citation>].

Mechanical impedance may generally depend upon numerous factors, including muscle activation, load or weight bearing, loading conditions, position or posture of the system (such as the joint angle), interface properties between the human body and the contacting surface, task, learning and training, and physiological conditions such as wellness, fitness, fatigue, and possible existence of various pathologies. <sentence_start/>Examples of the latter include recurrent low back pain, in which trunk stiffness was found to be higher and damping lower compared to the normal case [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR102" pmid="19062020" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2008.10.001" count="1">102</citation>], contrary to recurrent ankle sprain in which balance was not found to be impaired [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR27" pmid="9132216" doi="10.1136/bjsm.31.1.65" pmcid="PMC1332479" count="1">27</citation>].

Low back pain recurrence was also found to be related with lower stride-to-stride variability of trunk motion, resulting from a protective movement strategy, possibly based on increased trunk stiffness and damping [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR118" pmid="22078275" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2011.10.024" count="1">118</citation>].
Muscle Activation

It has been suggested that, mechanically, a muscle is analogous to a spring, whose stiffness is a function of its activation. <sentence_start/>As with a spring, a muscle’s force is a function of its length [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR119" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that in the limb joints, impedance can also be adjusted by the activation level of the antagonist muscles of the joint. <sentence_start/>Thus, for a required net torque in the upper limb, different levels of contraction of the antagonists will result in different impedance levels and, accordingly, in different energy costs of that net torque [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR115" count="1">115</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR120" pmid="17054964" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2006.08.007" count="1">120</citation>].

For the lower extremity, a high correlation was found between pre-contact EMG activity and the EMG activity in the concentric phase (brake phase) of the ground-contact period [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR121" count="1">121</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It was also reported that muscles can reduce the vertical peak ground reaction force due to their ability to absorb energy during impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR122" pmid="7601865" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(94)00127-p" count="1">122</citation>], and that recruitment and activation of stiffness proportional to initial stiffness can be achieved by positive muscle force feedback [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR123" count="1">123</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be remembered, though, that repetitive performance of a task may fatigue the active mechanisms of the human body [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR124" count="1">124</citation>].

It has also been found that in relation to minimizing soft-tissue vibrations, such as when energy dissipation is not desirable, impedance tuning is achieved by adjusting muscle activity in reaction to impact forces [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR125" pmid="15336933" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.01.002" count="1">125</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Prior to landing, muscle activity is responsible for generating the correct joint stiffness as determined by co-contraction of the muscles surrounding the joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR126" doi="10.1115/1.2746384" pmid="17655481" count="1">126</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In general, the central nervous system uses different mechanisms to tune the mechanical properties of the muscles to the different required tasks [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR127" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.1991.sp018596" pmcid="PMC1180048" pmid="1890636" count="1">127</citation>].

For the body trunk, to empirically evaluate the influence of coactivation on trunk stiffness, trunk dynamics, including stiffness, mass, and damping, were quantified during trunk extension exertions with and without voluntary recruitment of antagonistic co-contraction. <sentence_start/>It was reported that co-contraction increases trunk stiffness, thereby supporting the idea that co-contraction may contribute to spinal stability [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR128" pmid="16099678" doi="10.1016/j.jelekin.2005.06.006" pmcid="PMC1635026" count="1">128</citation>].
Impedance Tuning Through Pre-programmed Non-reflex Action: Pre-activation
Several factors have been reported to affect reduction of peak forces as a result of landing impact.

In repulsive tasks, impedance tuning through pre-programmed non-reflex muscle action during the early phase of impact helps reduce peak forces. <sentence_start/>The necessity of setting the joint angles and of tuning the stiffness before leg loading was reported [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR129" doi="10.1007/BF00636213" pmid="1592051" count="1">129</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In hopping exercise, the presence of an initial joint stiffness was found, suggesting that muscle pre-activation is important in controlling the peak forces [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR19" doi="10.1115/1.1590358" pmid="12968575" count="1">19</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be noted, however, that no direct information was provided about which leg muscles are part of this activity. <sentence_start/>For that purpose, EMG measurements should be taken in synchrony with the measured kinematics and foot-ground reaction forces. <sentence_start/>In a model that included wobbling masses to simulate the impact force peaks during running, it was shown that tuning of the muscle activation of the lower extremities alongside with changes of joint angles and joint angular velocities could result in controlling the impact force [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR130" pmid="10433427" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00048-2" count="1">130</citation>].

The pre-programmed non-reflex muscle action during the early phase of impact has been proven to be important in peak force attenuation. <sentence_start/>This procedure can be trained for and controlled by the subject to achieve simultaneous use of all joints and coordination between the various segments of the leg. <sentence_start/>Better attenuation is also a result of increasing the flexion range of the joints of the leg [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131" pmid="6889994" doi="10.1243/emed_jour_1982_011_039_02" count="1">131</citation>].

When deformation starts in passive mechanisms, a neurological feedback system senses the resulting increased force and so brings muscles into play before the forces have had time to reach destructive levels [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR132" pmid="317339" doi="10.1007/BF02443830" count="1">132</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The ability to pre-program muscle action and joint motion is thus of major importance when reflex activity has not yet appeared.

It should be noted, however, that the paraspinal reflexes have been shown to augment effective stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR120" pmid="17054964" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2006.08.007" count="1">120</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An increased reflex gain was reported following prolonged trunk flexion, which in turn may contribute to low back pain risk [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR133" pmid="15567532" doi="10.1016/j.clinbiomech.2004.09.001" pmcid="PMC1630677" count="1">133</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In fact, it has been shown that intrinsic muscle stiffness alone is insufficient for stability and that reflex dynamics are necessary components in the stabilizing control of spinal stability [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR134" pmid="16782106" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2006.04.018" pmcid="PMC1851677" count="1">134</citation>].

In the elbow and wrist joints, using a model with linearly time-varying angular stiffness and viscosity, it has been observed that anticipatory muscle stiffening and anticipatory flexion of the limb are synergistic in building up resistance of the hand to a catch task and that reflex coactivation produces a further increment of hand stiffness and viscosity to counteract the impact effect [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR135" pmid="2913200" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.09-01-00134.1989" pmcid="PMC6570012" count="1">135</citation>].
It should be noted that reflex mechanisms can be fatigued, as may happen with individuals performing repetitive tasks [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR124" count="1">124</citation>].
Weight or Load Bearing

It has been reported that the magnitude of the force acting on the leg affects its stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20" pmid="528546" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(79)90056-3" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Weight bearing on the foot was also found to influence mechanical impedance in torsion testing of the lower leg [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR72" pmid="7096375" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90254-8" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a large-scale pulse rotation test of the lower leg in which joint rotation was studied, it was noted that joint stiffness increased somewhat with weight bearing [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" pmid="3417692" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90146-7" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Increasing load was also found to increase the overall stiffness and damping coefficients in the subtalar joint [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>].
Conditions of Dynamic Loading

Impedance dependency with weight bearing, direction of perturbation, and displacement was reported in a large-scale pulse rotation test of the lower leg in which joint rotation was studied [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR71" pmid="3417692" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90146-7" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the dependency of mechanical impedance on perturbation frequency has been the subject of numerous investigations. <sentence_start/>For instance, the variation of dynamic stiffness and damping of the vertebral discs in the range of frequencies transmitted by a car seat has been reported [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR136" pmid="14605972" doi="10.1007/s00586-003-0569-0" pmcid="PMC3467989" count="1">136</citation>]. <sentence_start/>To simulate shock loading taking place during running, a multi-DOF lumped model of a standing human body was subjected to impulse inputs at the foot [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR96" pmid="9302670" doi="10.1016/s1350-4533(96)00081-1" count="1">96</citation>]. <sentence_start/>When comparing linear and nonlinear simulations, a significant decrement was found in the acceleration transfer magnitude in the nonlinear model and nonlinear damping was found to be significant. <sentence_start/>Subjects with higher body fat could have a greater degree of nonlinear damping, which provides better attenuation and higher energy dissipation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR96" pmid="9302670" doi="10.1016/s1350-4533(96)00081-1" count="1">96</citation>].

The loading rate of the impact force at heel strike, as applied by a pendulum on the foot, was found to affect muscle activation, as measured by EMG of the lower leg muscles [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR137" pmid="11509530" doi="10.1152/jappl.2001.91.3.1307" count="1">137</citation>].
Effect of Body Configuration

In standing posture, it has been shown that stiffness of the leg decreases with increasing knee flexion and is maximal in a fully extended knee [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR20" pmid="528546" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(79)90056-3" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the trunk, conversely, stiffness was reported to increase with flexion angle [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR133" pmid="15567532" doi="10.1016/j.clinbiomech.2004.09.001" pmcid="PMC1630677" count="1">133</citation>].

In impacting activities, among the factors that were reported to affect peak force attenuation as a result of landing impact, initial flexion of the joints plays an important role [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131" pmid="6889994" doi="10.1243/emed_jour_1982_011_039_02" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>During landing impact, high forces are imposed on the leg with the result that, if a low stiffness of the leg is desired (to reduce impact forces), a relatively high initial flexion angle of the joints is required. <sentence_start/>This, however, would considerably limit the range (amplitude) of flexion in these joints afterwards to effectively absorb the energy by the muscles spanning the joints. <sentence_start/>This latter point was quantitatively studied by evaluating the amount of elastic energy which could be stored and re-used in human hopping. <sentence_start/>It was concluded that the dissipated energy in muscles increased when the amplitudes of joint movements were larger [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR138" pmid="746378" count="1">138</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Utilization of stored elastic energy was reported to depend on the shortness in latency between the stretch and shortening phases of the muscles [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR139" doi="10.1007/BF00429744" pmid="499191" count="1">139</citation>]. <sentence_start/>If one is interested in dissipation of energy, such as during landing from a height, the bigger the range of joint angle, the better. <sentence_start/>Presentation of the muscle as an energy dissipating shock absorber as studied on the cat soleus revealed two prominent damping nonlinearities: motion amplitude and movement history dependencies [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR140" count="1">140</citation>].

Multi-joint flexion in activities of repulsive tasks is probably the basis for reducing peak forces at impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131" pmid="6889994" doi="10.1243/emed_jour_1982_011_039_02" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this case, proper coordination between the different joints is important. <sentence_start/>Increasing task complexity, as may be presented in multi-joint action, was shown to decrease efficiency [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR141" doi="10.1007/BF00430076" pmid="648508" count="1">141</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The reason for this is related to timing in multi-joint motion, which affects movement synchronization of the various segments of the leg. <sentence_start/>For the overall performance to be fully efficient, the acceleration maxima of the different segments should be in phase. <sentence_start/>It should be noted that correct action of the joints and muscles can achieve this effect even before the reflex activity has come into action.

Another example related to multi-joint coordination relates to sit-to-stand transition motion. <sentence_start/>Particularly, in people with pathology such as Parkinson’s disease, slowness of a sit-to-stand transition could be due to a reduced hip flexion joint torque and a prolonged rate of torque production. <sentence_start/>This could point to impairments in the ability to control sequential and/or coordinated movements of the joints [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR142" pmid="11921112" doi="10.1002/mds.10073" count="1">142</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR145" pmid="10840131" doi="10.1016/s0166-4328(00)00144-3" count="1">145</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It remains unsettled, however, whether motor deficits observed in subjects with Parkinson’s disease during chair-rise tasks are related to the lower limbs torques, and whether muscle weakness and rate of force generation impair the ability to tune the joint impedances.

For the upper limb joints, stiffness regulation was also reported to depend upon posture configuration [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR146" pmid="11914798" doi="10.1007/s00221-002-1049-1" count="1">146</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR147" pmid="12037183" doi="10.1152/jn.2002.87.6.2808" count="1">147</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One study on the upper limbs, with actively maintained elbow angles, showed that both the stiffness and viscosity increase with increasing elbow flexion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR148" pmid="3700435" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(86)90155-7" count="1">148</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In reaching motion, however, the value of hand stiffness depends not only on the joint angular stiffnesses but also on the geometrical configuration that the limb takes in space at any instant [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" pmid="4045550" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.05-10-02732.1985" pmcid="PMC6565149" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Rotational stiffness and damping were measured for the elbow extensor muscle. <sentence_start/>Stiffness was also found to depend on gender, elbow flexion angle, and co-contraction level while damping depended on the latter only [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR98" pmid="21484509" doi="10.1007/s10439-011-0308-3" count="1">98</citation>].

In studying the relation between posture and reaching movement, equilibrium of the upper limb is assumed to be reached at a position at which the length-dependent forces due to the opposing activations of the agonist and antagonist muscles are equal [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR119" count="1">119</citation>]. <sentence_start/>If this position is considered as an equilibrium position, it was hypothesized that reaching movements can be regarded as shifts in equilibrium positions [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR74" pmid="8423483" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.13-01-00045.1993" pmcid="PMC6576309" count="1">74</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This, however, somewhat contradicts earlier results about the relationship between movement amplitude and stiffness of the forearm movement that indicated that trajectory formation was more complex than a simple switch between equilibrium points [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR149" pmid="6502202" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.04-11-02738.1984" pmcid="PMC6564726" count="1">149</citation>].
Interface Between Body and Contacting Surface

Other factors affecting mechanical impedance include the body/support interface, such as footwear and terrain (e.g., ground stiffness) [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150" doi="10.2165/00007256-199826040-00005" pmid="9820925" count="1">150</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Static evaluation of the stiffness of various football boots in inversion-eversion motion showed that when using rigidly attached high boots, ligamentous load on the subtalar joint is reduced considerably [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR151" pmid="965424" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(76)90099-3" count="1">151</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The effect of footwear protection was pronounced in the elastic stiffness parameter in testing of the subtalar joint under sudden inversion motion [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR70" doi="10.1115/1.2891133" pmid="2308310" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Footwear was also indicated to be important in conjunction with speed when considering resonant vibration in soft tissue; it was reported to have a significant contribution to the energy dissipation after an impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR125" pmid="15336933" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.01.002" count="1">125</citation>].

Soft landing in jumping motion for the attenuation of peak force depends on the quality of the ground and of the shoes worn by the subject. <sentence_start/>A distinction should be made between voluntary landing and hopping motions; in the former, the muscle is transformed from a spring to a damping unit, intended to absorb and dissipate energy, whereas in the latter, the muscle stiffness remains positive [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR127" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.1991.sp018596" pmcid="PMC1180048" pmid="1890636" count="1">127</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, foam-rubber sheets on the landing surface can be expected to decrease the stiffness of the impact medium and thus reduce impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131" pmid="6889994" doi="10.1243/emed_jour_1982_011_039_02" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A study on the optimization of landing mat properties found that damping was far more influential in peak force reduction compared to stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR152" pmid="21162361" doi="10.1080/14763141.2010.524244" count="1">152</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The attenuation effect can be attributed not only to a decrease in stiffness but also to an increase in contact time during impact. <sentence_start/>For a given linear impulse, a contact time increase results in a decrease of the impulsive forces present. <sentence_start/>In one study on human running, it was demonstrated that a more compliant track increased the contact time of the foot with the ground [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR18" pmid="528547" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(79)90057-5" count="1">18</citation>].

Soft landing can also be achieved by landing on the balls of the feet to make use of the cushioning effect of the foot heel-pad tissue. <sentence_start/>The balls of the feet have a lower stiffness compared to that of the flat part of the foot [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR9" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, landing on the ball of the foot allows increasing the flexion range during impact. <sentence_start/>Landing on the balls of the feet considerably decreased peak forces as compared to landing with the feet flat [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR131" pmid="6889994" doi="10.1243/emed_jour_1982_011_039_02" count="1">131</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Also here, another contributing factor is the contact time; the longer it is, the smaller peak are the forces likely to result.

For a one-DOF inverted pendulum model representing the colliding leg in running, the natural frequency of the cushioning mechanism was estimated using linearized and extended Kalman filter estimators [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR153" pmid="21093865" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2010.10.041" count="1">153</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In this model, the stiffness and damping of the foot-surface cushion represented the fat pad layer at the bottom of the heel and the running surface. <sentence_start/>This stiffness is directly proportional to the estimated natural frequency. <sentence_start/>Thus, it has been suggested that leg stiffness is not directly related to running mechanics, but, rather, to the running environment [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR153" pmid="21093865" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2010.10.041" count="1">153</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In gait, the increased effective leg stiffness with speed supports the greater propulsion energy required before foot contact during faster gaits [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR31" pmid="21396646" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2011.02.072" count="1">31</citation>].

Testing of the coupling of footwear and the supporting ground confirmed that ground stiffness strongly affects the impact forces and that it should therefore be considered as an essential parameter in footwear design [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR154" pmid="19931083" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2009.08.029" count="1">154</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Ground stiffness and damping were also reported to influence hopping strategies through adjustment of the spring-like mechanics of the leg and surface combination to regulate the body center of mass and work output during exercise [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR155" pmid="16549093" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.02.011" count="1">155</citation>].

The dynamics of impact to the hip during a fall was studied during pelvis release experiments in which the dynamic response of the body to a step change in vertical force applied to the hip was measured. <sentence_start/>The simplest mathematical model capable of simulating the problem consisted of a single effective mass attached to three sets of spring-damper elements. <sentence_start/>The effective moving mass was located at the hip and one vertical spring-damper combination represented the structural properties of the skin, fat, and muscle within the contact area, as well as the compressive properties of the proximal femur, hip joint, and pelvis. <sentence_start/>The remaining elements were two horizontally oriented elements that consisted of the combined flexural stiffness and damping of the muscles and ligaments that span the spine and connect the pelvis to the trunk and lower limbs. <sentence_start/>These elements constrained the hips and pelvis from lateral excursions from the midline of the body [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR156" pmid="9146804" doi="10.1007/BF02684190" count="1">156</citation>].

For the upper extremities, the reduction of impact forces during forward falls onto outstretched hands was analyzed using linear models with surface stiffness modification. <sentence_start/>It was found that at the moment of impact, compliant surfaces attenuate the high-frequency peak force, which affects the wrist by decreasing the velocity across the wrist damping elements. <sentence_start/>At the same time, the lower-frequency peak deflection of the shoulder spring is not substantially reduced [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR157" pmid="9671925" doi="10.1002/jor.1100160306" count="1">157</citation>].
Task Dependency

The dynamic behavior of the motor system is considerably different from static behavior (where muscle stiffness behaves uniformly and consistently as springs) and it adapts to the requirements of the motor task [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR127" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.1991.sp018596" pmcid="PMC1180048" pmid="1890636" count="1">127</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For instance, during voluntary landing, the muscle is transformed from a spring to a damping unit, intended to absorb and dissipate energy. <sentence_start/>While muscle stiffness in the ankle joint is negative after touch down when landing, it always remains positive when hopping [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR127" doi="10.1113/jphysiol.1991.sp018596" pmcid="PMC1180048" pmid="1890636" count="1">127</citation>].

Dual tasking, combining postural control (inverted pendulum model) with outside distraction, leads to decreased stiffness and increased sway amplitude in the mediolateral direction by diverting the resources necessary for mediolateral postural control, thus increasing the risk to falls [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR158" pmid="20844110" doi="10.1152/jn.00820.2009" pmcid="PMC3007648" count="1">158</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It should be mentioned in this respect that an increased dispersion of sway in the mediolateral plane has also been associated with impaired vision and fall risk in the elderly [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR159" pmid="16311195" doi="10.1016/j.gaitpost.2004.11.018" count="1">159</citation>]. <sentence_start/>This group modeled postural sway during standing to retrieve the viscoelastic parameters of swaying motion using two methods: second-order oscillatory model and discrete second-order autoregressive model.

Impedance values were thus reported to depend on task constraints [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR160" pmid="9787002" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.18-21-08965.1998" pmcid="PMC6793558" count="1">160</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR164" pmid="11762234" doi="10.1007/s004220100277" pmcid="PMC2553889" count="1">164</citation>], the patterns of perturbation, and the actual joint movement configuration [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR10" pmid="4045550" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.05-10-02732.1985" pmcid="PMC6565149" count="1">10</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR146" pmid="11914798" doi="10.1007/s00221-002-1049-1" count="1">146</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR165" pmid="11889509" doi="10.1007/s00221-001-0968-6" count="1">165</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR166" count="1">166</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, in defining impedance characteristics, stiffness and damping coefficients have been mostly assumed to be variable [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR61" pmid="10529503" doi="10.1123/mcj.3.4.394" count="1">61</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR167" pmid="9691580" doi="10.1109/10.704874" count="1">167</citation>] with resulting dependencies upon deformation and rate of deformation [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR14" count="1">14</citation>].

In long-distance running, for instance, moderate speed may result in more than 300 foot strikes/leg/km. <sentence_start/>Each such foot strike evokes an impact loading that results in a vertical shock impulse transmitted upwards through the body and carries with it the potential for injuries in the bone and joint tissues. <sentence_start/>Fatigue or stress fractures occur in bones in response to repetitive stresses over multiple cycles when the body’s ability to adapt is exceeded [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150" doi="10.2165/00007256-199826040-00005" pmid="9820925" count="1">150</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR168" pmid="9213092" count="1">168</citation>]. <sentence_start/>An important factor that affects the incidence of bone stress injury is exposure to abrupt changes in the bone loading [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150" doi="10.2165/00007256-199826040-00005" pmid="9820925" count="1">150</citation>] and consequent alteration in the strain distribution [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR169" doi="10.1242/jeb.188.1.217" pmid="7964380" count="1">169</citation>] with insufficient recovery periods [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR170" doi="10.2165/00007256-199622030-00006" pmid="8883216" count="1">170</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Within the mechanical impedance parameters of the lower limbs, a major factor responsible for impulse attenuation at foot or heel strike is the shock absorption capacity of the active muscle in the lower limbs. <sentence_start/>Additionally, impact forces initiate vibrations of the wobbling soft tissues during the landing phase of running [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR171" pmid="19827473" doi="10.1123/jab.25.3.238" count="1">171</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR172" pmid="10653036" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00151-7" count="1">172</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The vibrations of these non-rigid masses, particularly those of the lower body, affect impact forces [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR172" pmid="10653036" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00151-7" count="1">172</citation>] and soft tissue vibrations and have been reported to contribute significantly to the energy dissipation after an impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR125" pmid="15336933" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.01.002" count="1">125</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR173" count="1">173</citation>].

During a running task, it was assumed that the properties of the model remain unchanged and the effect of mass and shoe hardness on the ground reaction forces was studied [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR172" pmid="10653036" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00151-7" count="1">172</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A modification on this model introduced a shoe-specific nonlinear function for representation of the ground reaction force, resulting in a better agreement between simulation and experimental results [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR174" pmid="17092510" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2006.09.016" count="1">174</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Later, by hypothesizing that the central nervous system keeps the level of the vibrations of the human body constant using muscle tuning, it has been shown that a wobbling mass model can correctly simulate the effects of shoe hardness on the vibrations of the human body during running [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR175" pmid="19883916" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2009.09.028" count="1">175</citation>].
Learning and Training

The level of preparation of movement coordination depends on the training stage of the subject [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR141" doi="10.1007/BF00430076" pmid="648508" count="1">141</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Training should not only prepare the subject for optimal use of the joint ranges but also to reduce the time difference between the segmental acceleration maxima to zero. <sentence_start/>Training was also reported to augment muscle stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR90" pmid="14659928" doi="10.1016/j.clinbiomech.2003.09.003" count="1">90</citation>].

The possible effects of learning over the time of conducting the experiments beyond the warm-up phase should be considered. <sentence_start/>Learning was reported to decrease joint total stiffness [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR11" pmid="10592022" doi="10.1007/s004220050577" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>While the training effect on stiffness was reported to be dependent on the training intensity [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR150" doi="10.2165/00007256-199826040-00005" pmid="9820925" count="1">150</citation>], when the training level was similar to the exercise level, learning usually took place within the first few sessions of training [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR176" pmid="17009492" doi="10.1109/TNSRE.2006.881591" count="1">176</citation>] and then leveled off, i.e., the difference between the test means in two consecutive sessions was not statistically significant.
Fatigue

Fatigue of the muscles affects not only their performance but other related functions as well such as unsteadiness of performance [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR66" pmid="7153228" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(82)90090-2" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It has been shown [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR177" pmid="3465203" doi="10.1111/j.0954-6820.1986.tb08943.x" count="1">177</citation>] that muscles act to lower the bending stress on bone and to attenuate the peak dynamic loads that can damage musculoskeletal tissues. <sentence_start/>Muscle fatigue has also been shown to affect the ability of the human musculoskeletal system to attenuate and dissipate the heel strike induced shock waves (for running [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR178" pmid="6447153" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(80)90340-1" count="1">178</citation>], for long-march [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR179" count="1">179</citation>]). <sentence_start/>Some studies [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR180" pmid="7391098" count="1">180</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR182" pmid="6814271" doi="10.1177/036354658201000507" count="1">182</citation>] have suggested that when the muscle’s ability to perform is diminished, the cartilage and ligaments become more vulnerable to excess dynamic loading, which in turn may increase stiffness. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, it has been claimed that, in direct contrast to experiments on whole body fatigue, localized muscle fatigue was found to cause a decrease in peak tibial acceleration and acceleration slope following impact [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR183" pmid="15288459" doi="10.1016/j.clinbiomech.2004.04.015" count="1">183</citation>].

In addition to muscle fatigue, metabolic fatigue may take place when the running subject exceeds a running speed termed the anaerobic threshold [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR184" pmid="4723033" doi="10.1152/jappl.1973.35.2.236" count="1">184</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR185" pmid="3119250" count="1">185</citation>]. <sentence_start/>With progressing fatigue in long distance level running, the effect on mechanical impedance can be inferred from the fact that the impact shock load on the lower limbs increases [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186" pmid="10590340" doi="10.1016/s0268-0033(99)00033-9" count="1">186</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR189" pmid="11415829" doi="10.1016/s0268-0033(98)00030-8" count="1">189</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One additional question is whether, as a result of fatigue, an imbalance between the activities of the plantar and dorsi flexor muscles of the ankle develops. <sentence_start/>Such an imbalance would further compromise the protective action provided by the muscles to the shank [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR190" count="1">190</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR192" pmid="10870903" doi="10.1114/1.284" count="1">192</citation>].

Measurements of the foot-strike-evoked impact at both the tibial tuberosity and sacrum levels by means of accelerometers demonstrated an increase of the impact in both locations with developing fatigue, indicating a diminished capacity to attenuate the foot-strike-initiated shock waves [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR189" pmid="11415829" doi="10.1016/s0268-0033(98)00030-8" count="1">189</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Time and frequency domain analyses of the acceleration data suggested that fatigue contributes to the reduction of the human musculoskeletal system’s capacity to attenuate and dissipate those shock waves. <sentence_start/>This capacity appears to be a function not only of the fatigue level, but also of the vertical location along the skeleton. <sentence_start/>It seems that higher up the skeletal, parts are able to withstand the effect of fatigue for a longer time.

In decline running, metabolic fatigue is less likely to develop compared to level running due to the reduced effort required for running. <sentence_start/>However, due to their eccentric activity, the major knee extensors do get fatigued, resulting in significantly increased shock acceleration at the sacrum level, while the shock acceleration at the tibial tuberosity remains unchanged [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR186" pmid="10590340" doi="10.1016/s0268-0033(99)00033-9" count="1">186</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, without metabolic fatigue development, shock propagation from the tibial tuberosity to the sacrum is augmented due to the eccentric action of the muscles.

Apart from the impact shock transmission, reported to provoke bone injury and joint damage, stride rate (frequency) at a given speed (i.e., stride length) was identified to affect stiffness. <sentence_start/>It was argued that a stiffer leg leads to a higher stride frequency and shorter stride length at a given speed [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR21" pmid="8849811" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(95)00029-1" count="1">21</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR22" pmid="10093026" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(98)00170-5" count="1">22</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR47" pmid="10569714" doi="10.1016/s0021-9290(99)00133-5" count="1">47</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR49" pmid="9729582" doi="10.1152/jappl.1998.85.3.1044" count="1">49</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Interactions between stiffness and kinematics were also noted, indicating that the impact shock can be attenuated by adjusting the joint stiffness and/or the joint kinematics, thus providing support for the concept of muscle tuning during dynamic activities and suggesting that speed/shoe combinations are important when considering resonant vibration in soft tissue [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR125" pmid="15336933" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2004.01.002" count="1">125</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR193" pmid="8945650" count="1">193</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR194" pmid="3610929" doi="10.1152/jappl.1987.62.6.2326" count="1">194</citation>].
Material Evaluation of Impedance (vs. System or Structural)

By direct in vivo and in vitro measurement of tissue segments, the passive viscoelastic parameters can be obtained. <sentence_start/>From quasi-static in vitro mechanical testing of vertebral bodies from the thoracic spine, flexibility and stiffness matrices from the load-displacement diagrams and the variation of the mechanical properties with the spine level were obtained [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR195" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(76)90003-8" pmid="1262353" count="1">195</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In vivo creep experiments of lumbar motion segment in centric passive tension during the course of hydrotherapy, using ultrasound for deformation measurements, revealed that stiffness and damping of these elements were gender- and age-dependent [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR196" pmid="15925372" doi="10.1016/j.jbiomech.2005.03.021" count="1">196</citation>].

Passive tests on the knee joint based on the free damped oscillation technique indicated that the passive viscoelastic properties were in a small range of values and invariant during the growth process of this body segment. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, the passive viscoelastic properties cannot be held responsible for abnormal control in human spastic paresis and cannot be used as a descriptor of spasticity [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR197" pmid="10521649" doi="10.1016/s0268-0033(99)00021-2" count="1">197</citation>].

Impedance of soft tissue (e.g., on limb surfaces) or hard tissue (e.g., forehead) has been measured by means of a loading device using the random force vibration method [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR198" pmid="3505301" doi="10.1007/BF02447330" count="1">198</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These investigators, however, commented on the difficulty of tissue impedance measurements because this impedance is small compared to the impedance of the measuring device.
Explicit Expression of Impedance of Contractile Tissue

To study the contribution to mechanical impedance of the muscle-tendon component by means of micro-structure-based phenomenological modeling, most early muscle models were used for investigating short term-tasks, such as distance jumping, high jumping, pedaling, kicking, and gait [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR199" count="1">199</citation>], typically lasting less than 2 s, with small interference of fatigue. <sentence_start/>More general muscle models should, however, include long-term dynamic features such as the force build-up within the muscle and fatigue effects.

Muscle and muscle-tendon system models have been proposed by several investigators [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR200" pmid="2676342" count="1">200</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR202" count="1">202</citation>], with the effects of the inner structure of the system explicitly expressed. <sentence_start/>In these models, though, an inherent difficulty is encountered due to the multitude of physiological parameters required. <sentence_start/>Some of these parameters are functional, e.g., rheological, describing the stress-strain relationships of the muscles and tendons [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR203" pmid="4256989" doi="10.1152/physrev.1972.52.1.129" count="1">203</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR206" pmid="3843415" count="1">206</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These types of parameters are referred to as muscle nonspecific parameters. <sentence_start/>The other types of parameters describe individual characteristics of the particular muscles modeled. <sentence_start/>They are associated mostly with the anthropometric measures of the individual muscles such as size, cross-sectional area, and mass of the muscles and tendons and are termed muscle-specific parameters.

The above five-element muscle-tendon model was also incorporated in the lower limb to enable long-term prediction of the force output of the quadriceps muscle during continuous electrical stimulation. <sentence_start/>In the contractile element, muscle activation was explicitly expressed by means of the EMG signal while muscle fatigue was incorporated by using a specially introduced term based on the concentration of intracellular pH [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR216" pmid="8244427" doi="10.1109/10.237696" count="1">216</citation>-<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR219" pmid="10659449" doi="10.1016/s1050-6411(99)00016-4" count="1">219</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The presence of fatigue during prolonged FES causes a substantial decrease in the force output of the quadriceps muscle [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR220" pmid="2319765" doi="10.1016/0141-5425(90)90136-b" count="1">220</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The metabolic parameters recorded using magnetic resonance spectroscopy [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="CR221" pmid="8419742" doi="10.1002/mrm.1910290111" count="1">221</citation>] revealed fatigue profiles (parallel to the force profile) when measured during stimulation and recovery profiles when measured after stimulation. <sentence_start/>These profiles served for prediction of the dynamic force in intermittent stimulation.
Conclusion

Tuning of the mechanical impedance is a major factor in asserting the sound performance of the many tasks assigned to the limbs and in counteracting undesired effects of applied loads and disturbances. <sentence_start/>It facilitates the control and stabilization of hand-held objects in space and their navigation in reaching motions as well as the attenuation of undesired shock loads resulting from externally applied forces. <sentence_start/>The ability to tune and/or control the mechanical impedance of the limb joints is not only an important feature of the neuromuscular system, but has also strong relevance in the design of torque-controlled manipulators and multijoint powered orthotics. <sentence_start/>In early works, impedance was conveniently assumed to be constant, resulting in linear models. <sentence_start/>However, more recent work has repeatedly demonstrated that linear models fail to predict the true dynamic response of modeled systems and that the use of constant mechanical impedance may not physiologically be applicable. <sentence_start/>Impedance nonlinearity is therefore required. <sentence_start/>An important reason is that impedance is intricately related to the mode and amount of muscle activation involved in the performance of as given task. <sentence_start/>It should be noted however that while estimating the nonlinear impedance component values, care should be taken to eliminate redundancies by reducing the model to reveal the correct and sufficient degree of impedance nonlinearity. <sentence_start/>For instance, in modeling grasping simultaneously taking place with locomotion, the spring coefficients should be expressed in terms of the joint angles and angular velocities, indicated a continuous nonlinear behavior of the joints. <sentence_start/>Both in the elbow and shoulder joints, stiffness includes a constant coefficient as well as an angular-velocity-dependent coefficient, with no damping. <sentence_start/>These results confirmed that a higher order of nonlinearity was not necessary. <sentence_start/>This result should be considered meaningful in problems where the constant stiffness representation is insufficient and in cases where the system’s representation has to be improved. <sentence_start/>This problem has strong relevance in impedance-based control strategies and provides insight into the mechanisms by which stiffness and damping are adjusted to accommodate changes taking place during simultaneous walking and manual transportation of objects, while aiming to ensure their stability. <sentence_start/>It also sheds light on the design of spring-based artificial and robotic arms. <sentence_start/>Another example is in tasks of repulsive loads, where the nonlinearity of the impedance of the leg joints is found to be expressible by means of a simple model, with a linearly variable stiffness. <sentence_start/>This enables the prediction of the major features of the jumping exercise, making it an effective tool for the future design of spring-based artificial legs and robots and the development of more accurate control strategies.
